deep.reconstruction:
This is the last page of E598. It holds two short corollaries closing the paper on divisors of numbers of the form p^2+nq^2 (prime divisors and quadratic forms). The opening of the next item, E599 (Solutio quaestionis ad calculum probabilitatis pertinentis), is printed on the facing page 315; that text is only its §1 set-up: 5% interest, lambda = 105/100, present value C/lambda^n.

Corollary 2 (§45). Euler says that the theorems on such divisors he had given in Comment. veter. Tom. XIV have become much more certain. These are E164, the 'Theoremata circa divisores numerorum in hac forma paa±qbb contentorum', which states the divisor classes by residues mod 4n. They are more certain now that Lagrange (Recherches d'arithmétique, 1773/1775) has proved the forms of these divisors. Euler expects that what is still missing will soon receive a perfect demonstration. This is in effect a forecast of a proof of the general residue-class description, i.e. quadratic reciprocity (Gauss 1801).

Corollary 3 (§46). The admissible residues a (mod 4n) of prime divisors of x^2+ny^2 are written with a sign, ±a with 0<a<2n. In modern terms the set H = {a mod 4n : chi(a)=+1}, with chi the Kronecker character (-4n/.). Because chi(-1)=-1, exactly one of a and 4n-a lies in H, so each odd a<2n coprime to n gets a definite sign. Euler observes that the first (1, always +) and last (2n-1) values determine the pattern. If 2n-1 has sign −, then a and 2n-a always have opposite signs. If 2n-1 has sign +, they always have equal signs. He illustrates with n=39 (77 is −, so the signs are opposite) and Example II, 2n=60 (59 is +, so the signs are equal). He says the reason 'can be found without difficulty' and that the remark lightens the labour of finding divisors.

Modern proof. For odd a with a·a' ≡ 1 (mod 4n), we have a+2n ≡ a(1+2na') ≡ a(1+2n) (mod 4n), since a' is odd. Hence chi(a+2n) = chi(a)chi(1+2n). Combined with chi(-1) = -1 this gives chi(2n-a)chi(a) = -chi(1+2n) = chi(2n-1), a constant. Moreover chi(1+2n) = +1 exactly when the conductor of chi divides 2n.
- For n=39 the discriminant is -39, the conductor 39 divides 78, so the signs are opposite.
- For n=30 the discriminant is -120, the conductor 120 does not divide 60, so the signs are equal.

I checked the n=39 list on the previous page against the rule: 1/77, 5/73, 7/71, 11/67, 17/61, 19/59, 23/55, 25/53, 29/49, 31/47 and 37/41 are all opposite.
errors: No mathematical error. The claim is correct and follows at once from the multiplicativity of the character mod 4n. Euler gives no proof ('haud difficulter inuestigari poterit').
On the previous page the sign of 35 in the n=39 table is not legible in the transcription. The rule forces 35 to have sign −, opposite to +43. This is consistent with chi(35) = chi(5)chi(7) = (+)(−).

ideas.what: Lagrange's proof of the forms of divisors makes Euler's E164 theorems more certain; a full proof is expected soon
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity / description of primes dividing x^2+ny^2 by residue classes mod 4n
ideas.where_published: E164 (Comm. Acad. Petrop. 14); E598 itself; Euler's late papers on divisors of quadratic forms

ideas.what: Sign symmetry a <-> 2n-a among divisor residues, governed by the sign of 2n-1
ideas.modern_name: chi(a+2n) = chi(a)chi(1+2n) for the Kronecker character (-4n/.); chi(1+2n)=1 iff the conductor divides 2n
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Dirichlet/Gauss character theory; standard property of quadratic characters
ideas.where_published: Euler noted many symmetries of the divisor tables (e.g. a <-> 4n-a) in E164 and later papers; I am unsure whether this 2n-reflection appears elsewhere

missed.claim: Euler states, without proof, that the sign pattern of divisor residues under a <-> 2n-a is uniformly equal or uniformly opposite, fixed by the sign of 2n-1. He leaves the reason as an exercise. In modern terms the dichotomy is exactly whether the conductor of (-4n/.) divides 2n.
missed.quote: cuius quidem phaenomeni ratio haud difficulter inuestigari poterit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically minor. It is an empirical detection of a property of the quadratic character, in effect conductor 4n versus a divisor of 2n, and shows Euler sensing character structure. It is not new mathematics today.

deep.surprise_reason: The page has a historical remark crediting Lagrange and forecasting a complete proof, plus an empirical symmetry observation that is an immediate consequence of quadratic-character theory. It is a nice early glimpse of conductor behaviour, but it is routine and likely noted in passing in Euler's other divisor papers.
transcription_corrections: §46: 'circa signa numerorum n' should read 'circa signa numerorum a' (the residues a, not n).
Page 315 belongs to the next item, E599, not to E598.
